teach.heading: Check the quality of your evidence
teach.body: A useful evidence note has a context, an action, and an observable result. “I organized people well” is difficult to test; “I asked each group member what they could finish, put the tasks on a shared checklist, and noticed one deadline was at risk” gives a reader something concrete. Then add a boundary: the event involved classmates and one deadline, so it does not prove the learner will enjoy managing a large team. Strong reflection includes what was hard and what support helped, not only praise.

teach.heading: Look for patterns without turning them into labels
teach.body: One example can suggest a question; several examples across different settings can suggest a pattern. If someone enjoys explaining a science demonstration and helping a younger cousin with a game, the shared clue may be adapting explanations, not “must become a teacher.” Ask what part of each task was satisfying, what conditions mattered, and whether the skill appeared again. A quiet learner can show communication through careful writing or listening; evidence does not need to look like public speaking. Use the pattern to choose a next experiment, such as comparing two roles’ daily tasks.

practice.prompt: Which note adds the most useful boundary to a skill claim?
choices: “I am naturally good at leadership.”
“In one three-person class project, I set check-ins; I still need to test whether I enjoy doing that repeatedly.”
“My friend says I should lead.”
“Leadership is a high-demand skill.”
feedback: This is a broad label without a task or limit.
Correct: it names context, action, and what remains untested.
Another person’s opinion is not direct evidence of task fit.
A broad labour claim does not show this learner’s experience.

practice.prompt: Two unrelated activities both involved explaining steps clearly. What is a careful inference?
choices: The learner must choose teaching as a career.
Adapting explanations may be a pattern worth exploring in more tasks.
The learner has proven expertise in every communication role.
The activities are irrelevant because they were unpaid.
feedback: Two examples do not dictate a single career.
Correct: the repeated action supports a hypothesis, not a verdict.
The evidence is narrow and cannot establish expertise across jobs.
Paid status is not required for transferable-skill evidence.

practice.prompt: A learner dislikes one part of an activity but likes another. What should the evidence record do?
choices: Hide the difficult part so the career idea looks stronger.
Name both the energizing task and the condition that made it difficult.
Discard the whole example as useless.
Treat discomfort as proof the whole occupation is unsuitable.
feedback: Selective evidence can distort the conclusion.
Correct: mixed evidence helps form better questions about work conditions.
An example can still show useful skills or preferences.
One activity is not equivalent to an entire occupation.

teach.heading: Separate typical work from entry requirements
teach.body: Profiles often combine tasks that occur frequently with requirements that apply only to some employers or specialties. Mark each statement as “typical task,” “legal or credential requirement,” “common preference,” or “one posting’s condition.” If the profile says a credential is required for a regulated occupation, verify that claim on the relevant Alberta regulator’s current page. If one employer prefers experience, that does not automatically make it a universal entry rule. A profile helps you build a research trail; it cannot replace checking the current rules attached to a specific role.

teach.heading: Use source disagreement as a question
teach.body: When two profiles disagree, compare the occupation name and code, region, update date, and the question each source answers. A national page might summarize a broad occupation, while an Alberta employer lists a narrow specialty. Do not average the statements or choose the one that sounds more encouraging. Record the conflict and identify a source closer to the decision, such as an official regulator for licensing or the program provider for admissions. If no authoritative answer appears, write “not yet verified” and ask an advisor before paying for training.

practice.prompt: A job profile calls a certificate “usually preferred.” A regulator page names a mandatory credential for a protected title. What should the learner do?
choices: Treat the phrases as interchangeable.
Verify the exact role and follow the current regulator requirement for the protected title.
Ignore both and rely on a social post.
Assume all jobs in the cluster require that credential.
feedback: Preferred and legally required do not mean the same thing.
Correct: confirm the exact title and use the relevant regulator for a legal requirement.
A social post is not an authoritative credential source.
One title’s requirement may not apply to every role in a broad cluster.

practice.prompt: Two sources give different training lengths. Which comparison is most informative?
choices: Compare their dates, program scope, and whether one describes full-time or part-time study.
Choose the shorter number.
Add the numbers and divide by two.
Assume the source with more pictures is newer.
feedback: Correct: scope and study mode can explain a real difference.
The shortest figure may describe a different route.
Averaging unlike programs creates a number supported by neither.
Visual design does not establish a publication date.

practice.prompt: A learner sees one employer preference in a current posting. What conclusion is justified?
choices: Every employer requires it.
It is evidence about this opening; check other postings and official requirements before generalizing.
It is legally mandatory.
No one can enter the occupation without it.
feedback: One opening cannot establish a universal rule.
Correct: preserve the scope of the evidence and continue comparing.
A posting does not itself establish a legal requirement.
The claim exceeds the evidence from one employer.

teach.heading: Compare more than the first payment
teach.body: A route comparison should identify when each cost occurs and which items are estimates. Up-front tuition, required equipment, application fees, transportation, housing, and time away from paid work can affect different learners differently. Keep one-time and recurring costs separate; a $400 tool purchase and $40 monthly travel cost cannot be compared by simply adding them without choosing a time period. Identify scholarships or paid training only when a current, eligible source supports them. If financing is needed, make borrowing a separate decision with its own total-cost and repayment analysis.

teach.heading: Check whether the routes reach the same destination
teach.body: Two programs may share a subject but lead to different credentials or scopes of practice. Trace the chain: program completion, any exam or supervised hours, registration or licence, then the actual job title. Ask the regulator or program provider which parts are mandatory, whether prior learning counts, and what happens if a learner pauses. Draw a decision point where evidence could change the plan. This protects a student from comparing one route’s introductory certificate with another route’s full qualification as if they were interchangeable.

practice.prompt: Route A lists $1,800 tuition, $250 tools, and $45 monthly transit for 10 months. What is the listed first-year total?
feedback: $2,050 omits all transit.
$2,095 includes only one transit month.
This does not follow the stated categories; use ten monthly costs.

practice.prompt: What makes an “alternate route” comparison fair?
choices: It leads to a related field, so the credential details do not matter.
Compare the actual title, credential, time, conditions, and additional steps each route requires.
Compare only which route has the lowest tuition.
Use a friend’s experience as the full program description.
feedback: Related work does not prove identical qualification or scope.
Correct: compare the destination and all route conditions.
Tuition alone omits time and other costs.
One person’s experience is useful context, not a complete official description.

practice.prompt: A program page and regulator page appear to conflict about entry. What is the strongest next step?
choices: Pay the application fee before asking.
Send the exact role and credential question to the program and regulator; record their current answers.
Assume the program page overrides all licensing rules.
Choose whichever answer supports the original plan.
feedback: Paying before resolving a key requirement risks avoidable cost.
Correct: ask the authorities responsible for the program and regulated title.
Program admissions and professional licensing are distinct.
Confirmation bias does not resolve the conflict.

teach.heading: Read the axis before the trend
teach.body: Before describing a graph, read the title, units, category, time window, and geographic coverage. A rising bar could represent a count, a percentage, or a forecast score; those do not mean the same thing. Check whether the vertical axis begins at zero and whether categories use matching definitions. If a report combines several years, note that it is not a current vacancy count. Copy the source name and retrieval date into your research notes so the claim can be checked later.

teach.heading: Triangulate without pretending to predict
teach.body: A second source is useful when it adds a different kind of evidence: current local postings, a provincial outlook, or an occupational profile. More sources do not automatically mean stronger evidence if all repeat the same old estimate. If one report suggests growth and current local postings are scarce, write both findings and consider season, region, commute, job title, and the date each was observed. Then state a conditional conclusion: “This is worth exploring if local opportunities and training costs remain workable.” Identify what new evidence would change that conclusion.

practice.prompt: A chart’s title says “projected openings,” but a learner calls the bars “jobs guaranteed to be available.” What was misread?
choices: A projection was treated as a promise of individual vacancies.
The learner included a citation.
The report’s region was recorded.
The axis units were included.
feedback: Correct: projected openings estimate a broader pattern; they do not guarantee a current opening for one person.
Citations help readers verify claims.
Region is important context, not an error.
Units help interpret a chart.

practice.prompt: A local search shows few postings over one week. What can the learner say?
choices: The occupation will disappear locally.
Few postings appeared in that search window; collect more evidence over time and check other channels.
The provincial forecast must be false.
No one is employed in the occupation.
feedback: One short search cannot establish future disappearance.
Correct: this is a scoped observation with a sensible next check.
Local postings and provincial forecasts measure different things.
A vacancy search does not count existing workers.

practice.prompt: Which evidence best supports a relocation question?
choices: A province-wide wage chart by itself.
A comparison of local openings, likely commute/housing costs, and relevant role requirements.
A friend’s guess about another city.
A national shortage label without a date.
feedback: A wage chart alone omits access and living costs.
Correct: it combines opportunity and practical constraints.
A guess is not verifiable evidence.
An undated label lacks context and may not match a location.

teach.heading: Trace prerequisites as a sequence
teach.body: A prerequisite is not only a course name; it is a dependency that affects when a later option can be taken. Draw a simple chain with the source and school confirmation beside each step. If a course is unavailable in a planned term, ask about the next offering, approved equivalent, or alternate route before deleting a career goal. Keep graduation requirements distinct from a specific college admission requirement. A school timetable and a university program page answer different questions, and both may need current confirmation.

teach.heading: Build a checkpoint around a decision
teach.body: Each route can have a “continue, revise, or investigate” point. For example, after reviewing the official admission page and meeting a counsellor, the learner can confirm the course sequence or identify an unresolved conflict. Record the date, evidence checked, and who can verify the next uncertainty. Avoid turning a grade threshold into a personal worth judgement: a result is information for choosing support or a different sequence. A backup route is strongest when it shares useful preparation and has been researched, not when it is simply a vague fallback.

practice.prompt: A student cannot access a required course in the planned semester. What is the strongest next step?
choices: Drop the pathway immediately.
Ask the school about later offerings, approved equivalents, and sequence effects before revising the route.
Assume an unrelated course will count.
Ignore the prerequisite.
feedback: A scheduling problem may have alternate solutions.
Correct: verify realistic school options and how timing affects later steps.
An equivalency requires confirmation.
Ignoring a dependency can delay eligibility.

practice.prompt: Why keep the source date in a high-school plan?
choices: Requirements, course offerings, and deadlines can change.
It makes a plan impossible to revise.
It proves admission is guaranteed.
It replaces checking with a counsellor.
feedback: Correct: a date helps identify when evidence may need refreshing.
Dated evidence makes revision easier, not harder.
A source date cannot promise admission.
School staff can confirm local sequencing and availability.

practice.prompt: Which is a useful checkpoint outcome?
choices: “I will see what happens.”
“After confirming the prerequisite and next course offering, I will keep, adjust, or research the route.”
“I must follow my first plan no matter what.”
“If I change the route, I failed.”
feedback: No decision trigger is defined.
Correct: this ties a decision to evidence and allows revision.
New evidence can justify a change.
Pathway revision is a normal planning skill.

teach.heading: Test customer need before estimating income
teach.body: A small business idea begins with a problem, not a guessed sales total. Identify who experiences the problem, how often it occurs, how people handle it now, and what evidence would show that a proposed service is wanted. An online poll of friends may reveal interest but not whether people will pay a sustainable price. Use a fictional trial or supplied data in this course; students should not solicit strangers, collect customer data, or spend real money to earn credit.

teach.heading: Calculate contribution, not just sales
teach.body: Revenue is money received before costs. A simple contribution estimate subtracts direct costs, but it may still omit permits, insurance, equipment wear, payment fees, tax obligations, and unpaid time. If a fictional service earns $150 and listed materials and transport cost $62, the remaining $88 is not automatically personal income or profit. List which costs were included and which were not assessed. Check current rules and adult supervision before any real venture, especially where a learner is a minor or the work involves safety risks. Ask whether the customer could choose not to buy and what evidence would distinguish politeness from demand. A route remains a hypothesis until cost, safety, and repeat interest are checked.

practice.prompt: A fictional service receives $210 and has $84 in listed material costs. What amount remains before any unlisted costs?
feedback: $210 is revenue before costs.
$84 is the listed cost, not what remains.
This adds costs to revenue rather than subtracting them.

practice.prompt: What does a positive remainder after listed costs establish?
choices: That the business is guaranteed profitable.
Only that revenue exceeded the costs included in that calculation.
That customers will return.
That legal and safety checks are unnecessary.
feedback: Unlisted costs and demand remain unknown.
Correct: the conclusion must match the costs actually counted.
Repeat demand needs separate evidence.
Rules and safe-work questions still need checking.

practice.prompt: Which is the strongest low-risk way to test an idea for an online lesson?
choices: Have students approach strangers with a sales pitch.
Use fictional customer feedback and a supplied cost sheet to compare options.
Require a real purchase.
Publish a student’s home address to attract customers.
feedback: Stranger solicitation is unnecessary and may be unsafe.
Correct: a simulation teaches the reasoning without exposing students.
Real spending is not needed for course evidence.
Publishing location data creates privacy and safety risks.

teach.heading: Use a capacity check, not a perfect-week assumption
teach.body: A weekly plan should include travel time, setup, transitions, meals, rest, and tasks that do not happen at a fixed hour. Mark fixed commitments first, then estimate realistic flexible time. If the plan only works when every bus is on time and no assignment takes longer than expected, it has no buffer. A simple calendar can reveal a conflict before a student interprets it as a motivation problem. Keep any personal schedule private; the lesson can use the fictional week supplied in class.

teach.heading: Revise the constraint that changed
teach.body: When a new constraint appears, separate the goal, route, and schedule. If a bus route ends earlier, a learner may keep an interest in a field but choose a local course, different work hours, an online option, or a later experience. Compare consequences and ask the school to verify options that affect graduation or admission. A revision note should show the original assumption, the new evidence, the chosen change, and a date to check again. It should also name the support needed rather than implying that the learner must solve every barrier alone.

practice.prompt: A plan has no travel or transition time and fills every evening. What is the clearest problem?
choices: It depends on a perfect week and leaves no usable buffer.
It proves the learner lacks commitment.
It will always work if the goal matters.
It should add more commitments.
feedback: Correct: omitted transition time makes the schedule fragile.
A plan constraint is not a character judgement.
Motivation does not remove travel or delays.
More commitments worsen an already full plan.

practice.prompt: A transit change makes the original route difficult. Which statement best separates goal from route?
choices: The learner must abandon the interest.
The learner can keep the interest and test a local, later, or online route with school confirmation.
The learner should ignore the transit change.
The original timetable is still valid without checking.
feedback: A transport constraint does not automatically invalidate the goal.
Correct: revise the means and verify feasibility.
Ignoring a known constraint weakens the plan.
Changed conditions call for a review.

practice.prompt: What belongs in a useful revision record?
choices: Only the new answer.
Old assumption, new evidence, change, reason, and next review point.
A statement that the first plan was perfect.
Private information about another family member.
feedback: Without the reason, the plan is hard to evaluate.
Correct: this creates a traceable decision and next step.
A plan can change when evidence changes.
Other people’s private details are not needed.

teach.heading: Check the exact category and exception
teach.body: A youth work rule may apply differently depending on the worker’s age, the type of work, the industry, school attendance, and the time of day. Before applying a summary, write down those facts and compare them with the scope of the current Alberta rule. Some occupations or tasks can have additional restrictions or permits. Never assume that a rule described for a 15–17-year-old also applies to someone aged 13–14, or that permission from a supervisor overrides a legal restriction.

teach.heading: Separate a schedule concern from a pay concern
teach.body: A schedule shows expected hours; a time record and pay statement help establish what was recorded and paid. If they differ, first compare the same dates, breaks, and duties. Keep a copy of the record and ask a specific question, such as “The schedule shows 6–10 p.m., but the recorded end time is 9:30; can we check the closing log?” For a real concern, consult current Alberta Employment Standards guidance or a trusted adult. A lesson calculation is not a legal ruling. Age-specific exceptions and work permits may matter for particular tasks. When official guidance is unclear, preserve the schedule and ask Employment Standards or a trusted school contact before treating a shift as permitted.

practice.prompt: Which fact is especially important when checking a youth shift rule?
choices: Worker age and the actual work/time conditions.
The colour of the uniform.
How confident the supervisor sounds.
What a different province allows.
feedback: Correct: applicability can depend on age and work conditions.
Uniform colour does not determine the rule.
Confidence does not replace the applicable standard.
Rules in another jurisdiction may not apply in Alberta.

practice.prompt: A recorded time differs from the schedule. What is the best first evidence check?
choices: Compare the same date, actual hours and break record.
Assume the schedule is always the final pay record.
Assume the employer intentionally changed it.
Change the pay statement yourself.
feedback: Correct: align the relevant records before drawing a conclusion.
A schedule is planned time, not necessarily the hours entered for pay.
A discrepancy needs investigation, not an unsupported motive claim.
Workers should not alter employer records.

practice.prompt: A summary conflicts with a current official Alberta page. How should a student proceed?
choices: Use the older summary because it is shorter.
Check the official page’s scope/date and ask an appropriate adult or authority if unclear.
Average both rules.
Choose the rule that permits more hours.
feedback: A short summary may omit exceptions or be outdated.
Correct: verify applicability and seek help with unresolved details.
Rules are not averaged.
Convenience does not determine which rule applies.

teach.heading: Choose a control that removes or reduces exposure
teach.body: Risk control is strongest when it eliminates the hazard or separates people from it, rather than depending only on reminders to be careful. For the unknown cleaner in the case, a learner should not touch, smell, mix, or pour it. Keep people away if safe, report it, and wait for someone trained to identify and handle it. A glove or mask is not a substitute for knowing what the substance is and whether that equipment is appropriate.

teach.heading: Refusal is a process, not a dare
teach.body: The right to refuse dangerous work is not an invitation to take risks or to confront someone alone. Tell the supervisor promptly, explain the specific hazard, and follow the current workplace and Alberta OHS process. The supervisor may investigate and take corrective action; the worker should not resume until the concern is addressed through the process. If danger is immediate, leave the danger area and follow emergency directions. The exact legal process and any exceptions must be checked against current official guidance. Never trade a worker’s safety for speed or customer convenience. A safe stop should be communicated promptly so the workplace can protect others and arrange trained assistance.

practice.prompt: Why is “wear gloves” not enough for an unidentified liquid?
choices: The correct protective equipment depends on knowing the substance and task.
Gloves make all chemicals safe.
Personal protective equipment removes the liquid.
The worker should test it by touch first.
feedback: Correct: without identification, you cannot know whether the glove is suitable.
Gloves do not protect against every chemical or exposure route.
PPE may reduce exposure but does not remove the source.
Touching an unknown substance creates exposure.

practice.prompt: What makes a control stronger than a reminder to “be careful”?
choices: It removes the hazard or reliably separates people from it.
It blames the least experienced worker.
It hides the hazard from visitors.
It assumes an injury will not happen.
feedback: Correct: controls should reduce exposure at the source or by separation.
Blame does not control risk.
Hiding a hazard leaves it present.
Assumptions do not prevent harm.

practice.prompt: A worker has reported the hazard but it remains. What is an appropriate response?
choices: Follow the applicable refusal process and do not resume until addressed.
Return because the supervisor heard about it.
Ask a classmate to test the substance.
Mix it with water to identify it.
feedback: Correct: report and follow the safe-work process; hearing a report is not itself a control.
A report does not establish that the hazard is controlled.
Another inexperienced worker should not be exposed.
Mixing unknown substances can create additional danger.

teach.heading: Choose the right reporting route for the issue
teach.body: A workplace can involve several distinct concerns: an immediate hazard, unpaid wages, schedule limits, harassment, or unsafe equipment. Start by naming the issue and its urgency. A safety concern belongs in the workplace OHS reporting process and may involve Alberta OHS guidance; a pay question may involve the employer’s payroll records and Employment Standards. Some situations need more than one route. Avoid sending a complaint to an agency that has no mandate for that issue, and seek a trusted adult’s help when uncertain.

teach.heading: Close the loop after reporting
teach.body: A report is more useful when it states what action is requested and how the worker will know whether the risk was addressed. For example, “Please confirm the guard is secured and show me the inspection procedure before I use the saw again.” Note the response and any change to the equipment or instruction. If the hazard persists, follow the escalation path rather than treating silence as resolution. Do not photograph coworkers or publish allegations online; preserve relevant records privately and use the workplace’s appropriate channels. Keep the report factual and limited to people who need to respond. A clear record helps identify whether a control changed and prevents the same hazard from being passed to the next shift.

practice.prompt: A worker reports an unpaid hour. What record is the most useful starting point?
choices: The time record and pay statement for the same period.
A photo of unrelated equipment.
A public post naming a coworker.
A safety data sheet for a cleaner.
feedback: Correct: compare records that show the hours and pay in question.
This does not address the pay discrepancy.
Public accusations do not establish the recorded hour and can expose private information.
A chemical document is unrelated to wages.

practice.prompt: A hazard report receives no response and the danger remains. What should the worker do?
choices: Treat silence as proof the risk is fixed.
Use the next appropriate workplace or official safety escalation route.
Resume the task to avoid inconvenience.
Delete the report.
feedback: Silence does not show the hazard was controlled.
Correct: an unresolved risk calls for the next safe reporting step.
Convenience does not make a hazard safe.
Keeping records can help a follow-up.

practice.prompt: Which report is easiest for a supervisor to act on?
choices: “The place is unsafe.”
“At 4 p.m. the guard shifted during the check; I stopped the task and need inspection before resuming.”
“Everyone knows the machine is bad.”
“My coworker is careless.”
feedback: This gives little detail or action.
Correct: it identifies time, observed condition, action, and requested response.
General reputation is not a checkable event.
It speculates about motive and does not describe the hazard.

teach.heading: Record facts without exposing others
teach.body: When documenting a concerning incident, keep an exact note of what was said or done, when and where it happened, who was present, and what decision followed. Separate a direct quotation from your interpretation. Preserve relevant messages privately and avoid forwarding them to classmates or posting names. A comparison can be useful, but only if it is fair: compare similar roles, qualifications, timing, and circumstances rather than assuming different outcomes have the same cause.

teach.heading: Seek a suitable and timely help route
teach.body: A trusted adult, school contact, workplace representative, or human-resources contact can help a young worker understand options. If the concern may involve a protected ground or a missed deadline, consult current Alberta Human Rights Commission information promptly because processes and time limits matter. An initial conversation can ask for criteria or clarification without forcing a learner to decide the legal label alone. In class, use the fictional file; do not submit a real allegation, another person’s identity, or confidential employment records. The learner does not have to confront the person alone. Preserve a copy of relevant information, note any immediate safety concern, and choose support before taking a step that feels unsafe.

practice.prompt: Which note best distinguishes fact from interpretation?
choices: “The manager hates me.”
“On Tuesday the training list was posted; my name was absent, and I was told applications closed Monday.”
“They always discriminate.”
“Everyone agrees the decision was unfair.”
feedback: This asserts a motive that is not directly observed.
Correct: it records a date, event, and stated reason that can be checked.
“Always” overgeneralizes without examples.
Group agreement is not a factual record of the decision.

practice.prompt: Why compare similar cases carefully?
choices: Different roles or qualifications may explain different outcomes.
Any difference proves discrimination.
Comparison is never relevant.
A comparison lets the learner publish coworkers’ records.
feedback: Correct: like-for-like context helps make the evidence meaningful.
A difference alone does not establish its cause.
Relevant comparisons can be useful evidence.
Private records should not be exposed.

practice.prompt: A young worker is unsure about a possible human-rights concern and a deadline may apply. What is wise?
choices: Wait until the end of the school year.
Consult current Alberta Human Rights Commission guidance or a trusted support person promptly.
Ask social media to decide the legal outcome.
Delete the records to avoid conflict.
feedback: Delay can risk missing time limits.
Correct: current guidance and support help the worker understand options in time.
Social media cannot determine the legal result.
Records may be needed; store them privately.

teach.heading: Translate experience into employer evidence
teach.body: A posting describes needs; an application should help the reader find matching evidence quickly. Choose a skill the role actually uses, then give one example with an action and result. A student who helped with a school fundraiser might describe how they checked the count against a list, spotted a mismatch, and asked the coordinator before changing the record. That example shows care and judgement without claiming paid office experience. Keep the example truthful and remove any names or private details about other people.

teach.heading: Make the evidence easy to verify
teach.body: Use specific verbs—checked, sorted, explained, repaired, planned—and avoid unsupported adjectives such as “perfect” or “expert.” If the result is not numeric, describe what changed or what feedback you received. A portfolio item can include a short reflection that names a challenge and what you would do next time. If the learner has no matching example yet, identify a safe practice task they can do in class rather than inventing experience or volunteering for an unsafe task. Use the same care when describing unpaid responsibilities: state the context and avoid suggesting that a project was a formal job. A clear boundary increases trust in the rest of the example.

practice.prompt: A posting needs accurate record handling. Which example fits best?
choices: “I am trustworthy.”
“For a class event, I checked the signup list against the kit count and asked the teacher about one mismatch.”
“I like computers.”
“My friend is good at records.”
feedback: This is a positive claim but no evidence.
Correct: it gives a relevant task, action, and appropriate response.
An interest does not show accurate record handling.
A friend’s skill is not the applicant’s evidence.

practice.prompt: The student lacks paid work history. What can they include?
choices: A truthful school, service, home, or project example described with an appropriate boundary.
A made-up employer and supervisor.
Another person’s private records.
Only a list of personality adjectives.
feedback: Correct: evidence can come from varied settings if accurately described.
Inventing employment is dishonest.
Private data should not be included.
Adjectives do not demonstrate the skill.

practice.prompt: Which verb makes a skill statement most observable?
choices: “I am amazing.”
“I reconciled the supply list with the returned items and flagged a difference.”
“I am destined to lead.”
“I have always been responsible.”
feedback: This is an unsupported evaluation.
Correct: the action can be pictured and followed up.
A prediction is not evidence.
A broad history lacks an example.

teach.heading: Use permission and privacy boundaries
teach.body: Workplace readiness includes knowing what you are authorized to do. A visitor asking for another person’s reservation, phone number, or schedule does not create permission to disclose it. Confirm the site’s identity-check and privacy procedure with the supervisor. If the procedure is missing, explain the request and ask for direction while avoiding confirmation that the record exists. The same principle applies in a simulated course: analyze only the fictional information provided and do not enter real names or records.

teach.heading: Match the response to urgency
teach.body: Classify a situation by immediate danger, privacy, deadline, and your authority. A spill blocking an exit needs an immediate safe action: warn others if safe, keep clear, and use the site emergency process. A printer delay usually needs a clear supervisor update and a proposed workaround. A learner should not improvise with unfamiliar equipment or chemicals. Tell the lead what is known, what is uncertain, what has already been done, and what decision is needed. If the supervisor is unavailable, follow the site’s escalation or emergency directions rather than guessing. The correct action depends on the urgency and the training already provided.

practice.prompt: A visitor asks whether a named person has a reservation. What response protects privacy?
choices: Confirm it if the visitor sounds confident.
Do not confirm or deny; follow the identity-check procedure or ask the supervisor.
Read the reservation aloud but hide the phone number.
Search personal social media for confirmation.
feedback: Confidence does not establish authorization.
Correct: avoid disclosure until the approved procedure is followed.
Even confirming existence can disclose private information.
Social media is not an authorized record-verification process.

practice.prompt: A spill blocks the only exit. What makes this different from a routine printer delay?
choices: It creates an immediate safety concern, so follow the site emergency process and keep people away if safe.
Both can wait until the end of the shift.
The worker should clean it without knowing what it is.
The worker should ignore the spill and finish setup.
feedback: Correct: blocked egress can create immediate danger.
The risk and urgency differ.
Unknown substances require trained procedures, not improvisation.
Ignoring an urgent hazard exposes others.

practice.prompt: Which supervisor update is most useful?
choices: “Something happened.”
“The printer stopped after one page; the 11 a.m. cards are incomplete. I can use blank cards if you approve.”
“The shift is impossible.”
“I fixed it” when no repair was made.
feedback: The lead lacks the task and needed response.
Correct: it gives status, consequence, and a proposed decision.
This offers no actionable detail.
Claiming a repair that did not happen is dishonest.

teach.heading: Match the story to the question asked
teach.body: A concise interview response begins with the question’s focus, not a memorized speech. For a question about change, identify the original plan, the new information, the action, and the result. For a question about a mistake, take responsibility for the part you controlled and explain what you learned, without blaming teammates. Use an example that is true in a real interview; this course’s fictional response is for practice only. Keep other people anonymous unless their details are necessary and authorized.

teach.heading: Turn practice into a conversation
teach.body: After drafting, check whether a listener could understand the context in one sentence and whether the result answers the question. Remove details that do not support the point. Practise aloud or in writing, but do not try to memorize a perfect script; follow-up questions may change the direction. Networking can also be a question-led conversation with a known adult or approved guest. Ask about ordinary tasks, training, and challenging parts. No student must contact strangers or share a personal phone number for course completion. A thoughtful answer can include a lesson learned without turning the response into an apology. Be concise enough to leave room for the interviewer’s follow-up.

practice.prompt: An interviewer asks how you adapted when a plan changed. Which answer fits the question?
choices: “I am hardworking and punctual.”
“When two volunteers cancelled, I reassigned the check-in task, updated the schedule, and we opened on time.”
“My group made me do everything.”
“I always succeed.”
feedback: These are traits, not an example of adaptation.
Correct: it gives a change, action, and observable result.
Blame does not show the applicant’s response.
An absolute claim is difficult to support.

practice.prompt: What is a good way to improve a spoken answer?
choices: Check that the result answers the prompt and remove details that distract.
Memorize every word and refuse follow-up questions.
Add private details about teammates.
Make the story more dramatic even if it changes the facts.
feedback: Correct: relevance and clarity improve the evidence.
Interviews are conversations; follow-ups are normal.
Other people’s privacy should be protected.
Changing facts undermines honesty.

practice.prompt: Which networking question helps a learner evaluate a role?
choices: “Can you guarantee I will be hired?”
“What tasks take most of a typical day, and what training helps a new person?”
“What is your home address?”
“Can I have your private account password?”
feedback: A contact cannot guarantee employment.
Correct: it asks about actual work and preparation.
Personal address is not needed and intrudes on privacy.
Credentials must never be requested.

teach.heading: Use a simple priority test
teach.body: When several tasks arrive, sort them by safety, privacy, deadline, and dependency. A task involving private records may have a strict permission boundary. An activity setup due soon may be urgent but can sometimes use an approved alternative. Ask what blocks other work and which decisions require supervisor authority. This is not a formula that replaces judgement; it gives a reasoned order and makes uncertainty visible. If safety is immediate, use the site procedure before trying to protect a deadline.

teach.heading: Review what the outcome actually shows
teach.body: A busy shift can produce mixed evidence: a learner may protect confidential information and meet a setup deadline yet report equipment failure too late. Write each observation separately, then identify one behaviour to repeat and one to practise earlier. Avoid “I am bad under pressure,” which turns one case into a permanent identity. A useful next test is concrete: send a short supervisor update as soon as a blocker threatens the deadline, then record whether the new timing helped. When two tasks compete, tell the lead early if one cannot be completed safely or on time. A timely request lets the authorized person reset expectations.

practice.prompt: Which issue should be handled before an activity deadline?
choices: A possible disclosure of private visitor information.
Choosing a decorative font.
Reordering unused supplies.
Writing a reflection before the shift ends.
feedback: Correct: privacy and authorization boundaries should not be crossed to meet a deadline.
This is a lower-priority choice.
It does not address an immediate privacy or safety concern.
Reflection can wait until the shift task is safe and authorized.

practice.prompt: The printer is broken and a deadline is near. What is a strong response?
choices: Tell the lead what failed, what is delayed, and propose an approved alternative.
Hide the failure and wait.
Use a personal account to access private records.
Claim the cards are printed.
feedback: Correct: early factual notice allows an authorized workaround.
Waiting can make the problem harder to solve.
A personal account does not authorize record access.
False reporting prevents appropriate help.

practice.prompt: The fictional shift went well in two areas and poorly in one. What should the reflection say?
choices: “I am a failure.”
Name the successful actions and a specific behaviour to change next time.
Ignore the feedback.
Assume the same result in every workplace.
feedback: One scenario does not support a global self-judgement.
Correct: specific evidence makes a useful improvement plan.
Feedback is evidence to examine.
Different workplaces and tasks can change performance.

teach.heading: Make the evidence chain traceable
teach.body: A portfolio claim should point to a record and explain the link. For example: “I want to explore public-facing work” can cite the fictional shift note where Rowan welcomed visitors, then note that the record also shows the learner needs to practise earlier updates when a tool fails. The next step could be comparing roles with different amounts of visitor contact and record work. A reader should be able to tell which part is observed, which is interpretation, and which is a future question.

teach.heading: Revise the plan without overcorrecting
teach.body: New evidence can change a detail, not necessarily an entire goal. If one task was difficult, ask whether it was a skill gap, lack of instruction, a work-condition mismatch, or simply a one-time problem. Choose a small next test to distinguish those explanations. A useful revision is reversible: research another profile, practise a supervisor update, or compare a second role. The supplied course records are enough to demonstrate this process; no signature or real placement is needed. A portfolio is not a prediction of employability. It is a record of current evidence and next steps, which can be revised as the learner gains more information.

practice.prompt: Which portfolio sentence is easiest to trace to supplied evidence?
choices: “I can work anywhere.”
“The shift record shows I kept visitor details private; I want to compare other roles with similar privacy duties.”
“I am bad at equipment.”
“My future is decided.”
feedback: This claim is too broad to evaluate.
Correct: it links an observed action to a next research question.
One printer problem does not prove inability with equipment.
The course emphasizes revisable plans.

practice.prompt: A learner struggled once with record work. What conclusion is most careful?
choices: All administration careers are unsuitable.
Identify whether the difficulty came from task interest, missing instruction, or a one-time circumstance and test further.
Ignore the evidence permanently.
Change every high-school course immediately.
feedback: One event cannot establish every role’s fit.
Correct: competing explanations lead to a better next step.
Evidence should inform further inquiry.
A large irreversible change is not justified by one event.

practice.prompt: What turns a reflection into useful career evidence?
choices: Task, action, result, interpretation, and a next check.
A supervisor signature only.
A confident prediction.
A long description without links to the source records.
feedback: Correct: the chain lets a reader see how the conclusion follows.
A signature is not the only proof and is not required for this simulation.
Predictions are not evidence.
Length does not replace traceability.

teach.heading: Check the goal amount and calendar
teach.body: A goal is easier to fund when its target comes from a current quote or a clearly labelled estimate. Break a large purchase into required parts: base cost, delivery, tax if relevant, and any recurring cost. Then check how many saving periods actually occur before the deadline. If the next pay arrives after a bill is due, a weekly average can hide a shortfall. Use a calendar, not just division, and label any amount that is invented for planning practice.

teach.heading: Keep the buffer’s job clear
teach.body: An emergency buffer is for unexpected needs, so define what counts in the fictional plan and how it can be replenished after use. The buffer does not need to reach an arbitrary amount before any other goal can begin; the appropriate balance depends on a person’s circumstances. For this online task, students can compare scenarios without revealing household savings. If a planned cost repeatedly uses the buffer, make it a separate target and revise the contribution schedule. A goal can also include a small contingency for price or timing changes. Keep that amount visibly separate from the target so the plan does not count one dollar twice.

practice.prompt: A target date is before the next scheduled contribution. What should the learner check?
choices: The actual dates and number of deposits before the purchase.
Only the weekly average over a year.
Whether another student saved the same amount.
Nothing; division proves the cash is ready.
feedback: Correct: the calendar determines whether deposits arrive in time.
A long-term average can hide timing gaps.
Other students’ finances are irrelevant.
An arithmetic average does not confirm available funds by the deadline.

practice.prompt: A school fee is due every September. How should it usually be planned in this lesson?
choices: As a predictable planned cost with a dated contribution target.
As an unexpected emergency every year.
As free because it repeats.
As a reason to ignore the emergency buffer.
feedback: Correct: a recurring known date can be planned in advance.
A predictable annual cost is not unexpected.
It still requires funding.
The buffer should retain its distinct purpose.

practice.prompt: The emergency buffer was used for an unexpected repair. What is a useful next step?
choices: Record the use and choose a realistic replenishment plan while protecting other priorities.
Assume the buffer must be replaced tomorrow regardless of cash flow.
Hide the use from the plan.
Borrow immediately without considering cost.
feedback: Correct: track the change and rebuild in a feasible way.
An arbitrary deadline may create another problem.
A plan should reflect the actual balance.
Borrowing has costs and should not be automatic.

teach.heading: Compare options using the same time frame
teach.body: Opportunity-cost reasoning improves when choices are compared over the same period and against the same constraints. If a learner spends $60 today, ask what goal contribution would otherwise have happened this week and whether that goal has a fixed due date. Do not compare one evening’s enjoyment with an entire year of hypothetical savings. A choice can be worthwhile if the learner understands the foregone option and accepts its effect on the plan. The goal is deliberate trade-offs, not a rule that every optional purchase is wrong.

teach.heading: Separate dollar effects from personal value
teach.body: A calculation can show how an extra payment changes interest under stated assumptions, but it cannot assign a universal value to rest, belonging, learning, or time with friends. Explain both kinds of reason separately. For a fictional choice, state the amount and which goal changes, then explain why the selected benefit matters to that person. A different learner may choose differently with different priorities. Avoid grading students on whether they choose the teacher’s preferred lifestyle; assess whether they recognize the trade-off and support the decision.

practice.prompt: A learner’s $40 choice delays a goal by one week. What is the most complete comparison?
choices: Name the $40, the delayed deposit/date, and why the chosen benefit is worth that trade-off.
Say the choice is wrong because saving always wins.
Ignore the goal deadline.
Convert friendship into an invented dollar value.
feedback: Correct: this states the financial consequence and personal reason.
There is no universal rule that saving always wins.
The timing consequence is central to the trade-off.
Personal value cannot be reliably reduced to a made-up dollar figure.

practice.prompt: Two uses of money are being compared. Which setup is fairest?
choices: Use the same period and include the goal deadline and constraints.
Compare one purchase with a ten-year investment projection.
Ignore fees in one option but include them in the other.
Choose whichever option has a larger label.
feedback: Correct: matching period and constraints makes the comparison meaningful.
The time horizons differ.
The assumptions are inconsistent.
A product label does not establish value.

practice.prompt: Why is opportunity cost not always a precise dollar amount?
choices: Some forgone benefits, such as rest or connection, are meaningful but not objectively priced.
Because all choices have identical costs.
Because calculations are never useful.
Because preferences should not affect decisions.
feedback: Correct: some benefits are qualitative and should be explained rather than fabricated.
Choices can have different consequences.
Calculations help with numerical effects; they have limits.
Personal priorities are part of an informed decision.

teach.heading: Read the terms that affect access
teach.body: A comparison should identify when the learner can withdraw, whether there are transaction limits, whether a promotional rate expires, and what fees apply after the promotion. Note whether a rate is variable or fixed only when current product documentation says so. A posted annual rate does not explain every condition, and a high starting rate may not last through the goal date. Keep the date of the product page because providers can change terms. In class, use the supplied fictional offer rather than opening an account or sharing a real statement.

teach.heading: Match the risk to the deadline
teach.body: Ask what happens if the value is lower on the date the money is needed. A deposit balance and a market investment do not have identical risks or protections. A near-term emergency goal often values access and predictable balance; a long-horizon goal may allow a learner to study investments, but can still experience loss. Do not infer that a registered account guarantees the investments inside it, or that a product is suitable because it appears in a familiar account. Verify current official protections and eligibility before making a real claim.

practice.prompt: A promotional rate ends before the goal date. Which comparison matters next?
choices: The ongoing rate, fees, access conditions, and value after promotion.
The banner colour.
The opening rate alone.
The provider’s slogan.
feedback: Correct: the learner needs the terms that apply when funds remain invested.
Design does not change the terms.
The initial rate may not last.
A slogan does not establish value or access.

practice.prompt: Which statement about a registered account and investment is sound?
choices: The account label guarantees every investment inside it cannot lose value.
An account arrangement and the assets held within it have different features and risks.
All eligible accounts hold only cash.
A familiar account name proves tax treatment for every person.
feedback: The account does not guarantee an investment’s value.
Correct: distinguish the wrapper/account from the held product or asset.
Different arrangements may permit different holdings.
Eligibility and tax treatment depend on current rules and circumstances.

practice.prompt: A learner needs emergency money soon. What feature deserves close attention?
choices: Access timing, withdrawal conditions, and fees.
Only the highest advertised return.
Whether the investment performed well in a past year.
How popular the product is online.
feedback: Correct: access is central for a near-term need.
A high return claim may ignore access and risk.
Past performance does not guarantee the future or establish suitability.
Popularity is not evidence of fit.

notes: Career, youth-employment, occupational licensing, human-rights, and workplace-safety details can change or depend on age, role, industry, and jurisdiction. Recheck current Alberta government, regulator, and school guidance before release; packets teach evidence-seeking rather than determining real cases.

Financial examples in FL3 expansions are fictional practice values only. Any real account, rate, fee, eligibility, protection, or tax statement should be checked against current official provider or Canadian government sources before release.
All added scenarios are fictional. Learners should not disclose real schedules, job records, workplace complaints, customer information, or personal financial details.
